at blive bange.explanation: "At blive bange" means "to get scared". When you name what scares you, add "for" (of): "Han blev bange for hunden" (He got scared of the dog). Do not mix it up with "at være bange" (to be scared), which says you are scared right now: "Jeg er bange for hunde" (I am scared of dogs).

at blive enige.explanation: "At blive enige" means "to agree". When you name what you agree on, add "om" (on): "Vi blev enige om at tage toget" (We agreed to take the train). When one person says they share an opinion, use "at være enig" (to agree) instead: "Jeg er enig" (I agree).

at blive forelsket.explanation: "At blive forelsket" means "to fall in love". When you name the person, use "i" (in): "Hun blev forelsket i sin kollega" (She fell in love with her coworker). When you say you are in love right now, use "at være forelsket" (to be in love): "Jeg er forelsket" (I am in love).

at blive færdig.explanation: "At blive færdig" means "to finish / graduate". When you finish a task, add "med" (with) and the task: "Jeg blev færdig med lektierne" (I finished the homework). When you graduate in a profession, add "som" (as): "Hun bliver færdig som læge" (She is graduating as a doctor).

at blive gammel.explanation: "At blive gammel" means "to grow old". The verb "blive" (to become) also goes with other adjectives. When you say something gets cold, use "at blive kold" (to get cold). When you say something gets big, use "at blive stor" (to grow big).

at blive gift.explanation: "At blive gift" means "to get married". When you name the person you marry, use "med" (with): "at blive gift med ham" (to marry him). When you say you are married right now, use "at være gift" (to be married): "Jeg er gift" (I am married).

at blive glad.explanation: "At blive glad" means "to become happy". When you name what made you happy, add "for" (about): "Jeg blev glad for kagen" (I was happy about the cake). When you say you are happy right now, use "at være glad" (to be happy): "Jeg er glad" (I am happy).

at blive hjemme.explanation: "At blive hjemme" means "to stay home". Do not mix up "hjemme" (at home) and "hjem" (home). "Hjemme" says where you are: "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home). "Hjem" says where you go: "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). In "at blive syg" (to get sick), the verb "blive" means "to become": "Jeg blev syg" (I got sick).

at blive indlagt.explanation: "At blive indlagt" means "to be hospitalized". When you name the illness, add "med" (with): "Jeg blev indlagt med lungebetændelse" (I was hospitalized with pneumonia). When you name the place, add "på" (at): "Han blev indlagt på hospitalet" (He was admitted to the hospital).

at blive optaget.explanation: "At blive optaget" means "to be admitted". When you get a place at a school or a club after applying, use it: "Hun blev optaget i klubben" (She was admitted to the club). When a sound is recorded, "optaget" means "recorded": "Samtalen blev optaget" (The conversation was recorded).

at blive rask.explanation: "At blive rask" means "to get better", as in recovering from an illness. When you say someone is well again, use "rask" (well): "Hun er rask igen" (She is well again). When you wish someone who is ill a quick recovery, say "God bedring!" (Get well soon!)

at blive skilt.explanation: "At blive skilt" means "to get divorced". When you name the person you divorce, add "fra" (from): "Hun blev skilt fra sin mand" (She got divorced from her husband). When you describe a person's current status, use "fraskilt" (divorced): "Han er fraskilt" (He is divorced).

at blive syg.explanation: "At blive syg" means "to get sick". When you say you are sick right now, use "at være syg" (to be sick): "Hun er syg" (She is sick).

at blive til.explanation: "At blive til" means "to become / turn into". When one thing changes into another, put "til" (into) before the new thing: "Larven blev til en sommerfugl" (The caterpillar turned into a butterfly). When you say how someone feels, leave out "til": "Han blev træt" (He got tired).

at blive træt.explanation: "At blive træt" means "to get tired". When you say you are tired right now, use "at være træt" (to be tired): "Jeg er træt" (I am tired).

at blive udskrevet.explanation: "At blive udskrevet" means "to be discharged", as in leaving the hospital. It is built from "ud" (out) and "at skrive" (to write). When a doctor writes out a prescription, the verb "at udskrive" is used: "Lægen udskrev en recept" (The doctor wrote out a prescription).

at blive uvenner.explanation: "At blive uvenner" means "to fall out", as in stopping being friends. It is built from "u-" (not) and "venner" (friends). When you name the other person, add "med" (with): "Jeg blev uvenner med min nabo" (I fell out with my neighbor).

at blive væk.explanation: "At blive væk" means "to stay away / go missing". When someone does not come to an event, add "fra" (from): "Han blev væk fra mødet" (He stayed away from the meeting). When you cannot find an object, use the verb about the object: "Min nøgle er blevet væk" (My key has gone missing).

at blokere.explanation: "At blokere" means "to block". When you stop a phone number from reaching you, use the same verb: "Jeg har blokeret hans nummer" (I have blocked his number).

at blomstre.explanation: "At blomstre" means "to bloom". It is built from "blomst" (flower). When you say a town or a business is doing well, the same verb means "to thrive": "Byen blomstrer" (The town is thriving).

at blotlægge.explanation: "At blotlægge" means "to expose". It is built from "blot" (bare) and "at lægge" (to lay), so literally it is "to lay bare". When something physical becomes visible, use it: "Regnen blotlagde rødderne" (The rain exposed the roots).

at bluffe.explanation: "At bluffe" means "to bluff". When someone pretends to know something outside a game, use the same verb: "Han bluffer, når han siger, at han kan fransk" (He is bluffing when he says he knows French).

at blive vred.explanation: "At blive vred" means "to get angry". When you name the person you are angry at, add "på" (at): "Jeg blev vred på min bror" (I got angry at my brother). When you say you are angry right now, use "at være vred" (to be angry): "Han er vred" (He is angry).

at blæse.explanation: "At blæse" means "to blow". When you blow with your mouth, name what you blow: "Jeg blæser lysene ud" (I blow the candles out). When you do not care about something, use "på" (on): "Det blæser jeg på" (I do not care about that).

at bo.explanation: "At bo" means "to live (somewhere)". When you say where you live, add "i" (in) and the place: "Jeg bor i Aarhus" (I live in Aarhus). Do not mix it up with "at leve" (to be alive): "Min farmor lever stadig" (My grandmother is still alive).

at bo sammen.explanation: "At bo sammen" means "to live together". When you name who you live with, add "med" (with): "Jeg bor sammen med min bror" (I live together with my brother). Without "sammen" (together), "at bo" (to live somewhere) only says where you live: "Jeg bor i Aarhus" (I live in Aarhus).

at bokse.explanation: "At bokse" means "to box", as a sport. The sport itself is "boksning" (boxing). When you say you do the sport as a hobby, use "at gå til" (to go to): "Jeg går til boksning" (I do boxing).

at booke.explanation: "At booke" means "to book", as in reserving. The word comes from English. When you reserve a place to sleep, name it: "Jeg har booket et hotelværelse" (I have booked a hotel room).

at bore.explanation: "At bore" means "to drill". The power tool is "en boremaskine" (a drill), built from "bore" and "maskine" (machine).

at bortføre.explanation: "At bortføre" means "to abduct". It is built from "bort" (away) and "at føre" (to lead). To say a person was abducted, use "blive bortført" (to be abducted): "Barnet blev bortført i går" (The child was abducted yesterday).

at bremse.explanation: "At bremse" means "to slow down". When you stop a vehicle with the brakes, it means "to brake": "Han bremsede hårdt på cyklen" (He braked hard on his bike). When something holds you back, use it too: "Regnen bremser os" (The rain slows us down).

at bringe.explanation: "At bringe" means "to bring". When you carry something along with you, you can use "at tage med" (to take along): "Jeg tager kaffe med" (I am bringing coffee). In the phrase "bringe i fare" (to put in danger), name who is in danger: "Han bragte os i fare" (He put us in danger).

at brokke sig.explanation: "At brokke sig" means "to complain / grumble". Add "over" (about) for what bothers you: "Vi brokker os over støjen" (We complain about the noise).

at bruge.explanation: "At bruge" means "to use". When you spend money, the same verb is used: "Jeg bruger mange penge på mad" (I spend a lot of money on food). When you spend time, it works too: "Jeg brugte to timer på lektierne" (I spent two hours on the homework).

at bruge op.explanation: "At bruge op" means "to use up". The small word "op" (up) adds the idea of finishing, as in "at spise op" (to eat up) and "at drikke op" (to drink up). Do not mix it up with "at bruge" (to use), which does not say that nothing is left: "Jeg bruger en kniv" (I use a knife).

at bruge penge.explanation: "At bruge penge" means "to spend money". The word "penge" (money) has no article, so do not put "en" or "et" before it: "Jeg har penge" (I have money).

at bryde.explanation: "At bryde" means "to break". When you do not keep a promise, use it: "Han brød sit løfte" (He broke his promise). When a quiet moment ends because someone speaks, use it too: "Hun brød stilheden" (She broke the silence). Do not mix up "brød" (broke) with "et brød" (a loaf of bread): "Jeg køber et brød" (I buy a loaf of bread).

at bryde et løfte.explanation: "At bryde et løfte" means "to break a promise". When you break a rule instead, the verb stays the same: "at bryde en regel" (to break a rule). Do not mix up "et løfte" (a promise) with "at løfte" (to lift): "Jeg løfter kassen" (I lift the box).

at bryde loven.explanation: "At bryde loven" means "to break the law". When a cup or a toy breaks, use "at gå i stykker" (to break) instead: "Koppen gik i stykker" (The cup broke).

at brække.explanation: "At brække" means "to break (a bone)". When you hurt a bone, name it: "Hun brækkede armen" (She broke her arm). With "sig" (yourself), it means "to vomit": "Han brækkede sig" (He threw up). When a glass or plate breaks, use "at gå i stykker" (to break): "Glasset gik i stykker" (The glass broke).

at brænde.explanation: "At brænde" means "to burn". When food stays too long in the oven or pan, use it: "Jeg brændte brødet" (I burned the bread). When you hurt your skin on something hot, use it too: "Jeg brændte min hånd" (I burned my hand).

at brænde ud.explanation: "At brænde ud" means "to burn out". When a candle burns until nothing is left, use it: "Stearinlyset brændte ud" (The candle burned out). When a person is worn out from too much work, use it too: "Han er brændt ud" (He has burned out).

at brøle.explanation: "At brøle" means "to roar". When people laugh very loudly, use "af" (with): "Vi brølede af grin" (We roared with laughter).

at bukke.explanation: "At bukke" means "to bow". Do not mix it up with "at bukke sig" (to bend down): "Jeg bukker mig for at samle pennen op" (I bend down to pick up the pen).

at bukke sig.explanation: "At bukke sig" means "to bend down". The word "sig" (yourself) separates it from "at bukke" (to bow): "Han bukker for publikum" (He bows to the audience). When you bend down for something, add "efter" (for): "Jeg bukker mig efter nøglen" (I bend down for the key).

at burde.explanation: "At burde" means "ought to / should". When you say what someone ought to do, use "bør" or "burde": "Du bør hvile dig" (You ought to rest). Do not mix it up with "at skulle" (to have to): "Du skal hvile dig" (You have to rest).

related.en: to have no choice but to

at byde.explanation: "At byde" means "to offer / bid". When you offer food or drink, add "på" (on): "Må jeg byde på en kop kaffe?" (May I offer you a cup of coffee?) When you say how much you bid, put the amount right after the verb: "Jeg byder tusind kroner" (I bid a thousand kroner).

at byde velkommen.explanation: "At byde velkommen" means "to welcome". It is built from "at byde" (to offer) and "velkommen" (welcome). To name the place, add "til" (to): "Vi byder dig velkommen til Danmark" (We welcome you to Denmark).

at bygge.explanation: "At bygge" means "to build". When you make a structure, name it after the verb: "Han bygger en garage" (He is building a garage). When you say a story rests on facts, add "på" (on): "Filmen bygger på en sand historie" (The film is based on a true story).

at bygge om.explanation: "At bygge om" means "to rebuild / convert". The small word "om" adds the idea of doing something over in a new way, as in "at lave om" (to redo) and "at flytte om" (to rearrange). When you change a building for a new use, add "til" (into): "De byggede laden om til et hus" (They converted the barn into a house).

at bygge på.explanation: "At bygge på" means "to build on / add on". When you add a new part to a building, use it: "De byggede en ny etage på" (They added a new floor). When you say a film rests on a book, it means "to be based on": "Filmen bygger på en bog" (The film is based on a book).

at bytte.explanation: "At bytte" means "to exchange". When you ask someone to swap places with you, use it: "Vil du bytte plads?" (Do you want to swap seats?)

at bære.explanation: "At bære" means "to carry / wear". When you say what clothes you have on, you can use "at have på" (literally, "to have on"): "Jeg har en jakke på" (I am wearing a jacket).

at bøje.explanation: "At bøje" means "to bend". When you bend an object, name it: "Han bøjede grenen" (He bent the branch). When you bend your own body down, add "mig" (myself): "Jeg bøjer mig" (I bend down).

at børste tænder.explanation: "At børste tænder" means "to brush teeth". Danish leaves out "mine" (my), so you say just "tænder" (teeth): "Har du børstet tænder?" (Have you brushed your teeth?)

at bøvse.explanation: "At bøvse" means "to burp". The matching noun is "en bøvs" (a burp).

bacon.explanation: "Bacon" means "bacon". Do not mix it up with "skinke" (ham): "Jeg har skinke på brødet" (I have ham on the bread).

badebukser.explanation: "Badebukser" means "swim trunks". It is built from "bade" (bathing) and "bukser" (pants). It is plural, so use "mine" (my), not "min": "Jeg har glemt mine badebukser" (I forgot my swim trunks).

badetøj.explanation: "Badetøj" means "swimwear". It is built from "bade" (bathing) and "tøj" (clothes). This word has no article, so leave out "et": "Jeg har badetøj med" (I have swimwear with me).

badminton.explanation: "Badminton" means "badminton". When you say you do the sport as a hobby, use "at gå til" (to go to): "Jeg går til badminton om tirsdagen" (I do badminton on Tuesdays).

bag.explanation: "Bag" means "behind". It always needs a thing after it: "bag bilen" (behind the car). When you name nothing, use "bagved" (at the back) instead: "Katten sidder bagved" (The cat is sitting at the back).

bagage.explanation: "Bagage" means "luggage". This word has no article, so leave out "en": "Min bagage er tung" (My luggage is heavy). When you talk about one specific kind of luggage, use its name: "en kuffert" (a suitcase).

bagefter.explanation: "Bagefter" means "afterwards". When you say what happens next, it stands alone: "Vi spiser, og bagefter ser vi film" (We eat, and afterwards we watch a film). When you name the thing that something follows, use "efter" (after) instead: "efter maden" (after the meal).

bagepapir.explanation: "Bagepapir" means "baking paper". It is built from "bage" (to bake) and "papir" (paper).

bagepulver.explanation: "Bagepulver" means "baking powder". It is built from "bage" (to bake) and "pulver" (powder).

bagfra.explanation: "Bagfra" means "from behind". It is built from "bag" (behind) and "fra" (from). When you see someone from the back, say: "Jeg så ham bagfra" (I saw him from behind). When you name the place where something is, use "bag" (behind): "bag huset" (behind the house).

baglæns.explanation: "Baglæns" means "backwards". When you describe how someone moves, put it after the verb: "Han går baglæns" (He walks backwards). When you tell someone to return to where they were, use "tilbage" (back): "Gå tilbage!" (Go back!)

bagom.explanation: "Bagom" means "around behind". It is built from "bag" (behind) and "om" (around). When you go to the back of a place, use it with a verb of movement: "Han cyklede bagom skolen" (He cycled around behind the school). For a spot where something simply is, use "bag" (behind): "Katten sidder bag døren" (The cat sits behind the door).

bagt.explanation: "Bagt" means "baked". It comes from the verb "at bage" (to bake). Do not mix it up with "stegt" (fried): "stegte æg" (fried eggs).

bagud.explanation: "Bagud" means "be behind". When you say you are late with something, add "med" (with): "Han er bagud med huslejen" (He is behind on the rent). For where something sits, use "bag" (behind): "Hunden ligger bag sofaen" (The dog lies behind the sofa).

ballade.explanation: "En ballade" means "a fuss". To say someone is making a fuss, use "at lave ballade" (to make trouble): "Børnene laver ballade" (The children are making trouble).

balsam.explanation: "En balsam" means "a conditioner". When you say what you use after washing your hair, say: "Jeg bruger balsam efter hårvask" (I use conditioner after washing my hair).

bange.explanation: "Bange" means "afraid". To name the thing you fear, add "for" (of): "Hun er bange for edderkopper" (She is afraid of spiders). To calm someone, say "Vær ikke bange!" (Do not be afraid!)

bange for.explanation: "Bange for" means "afraid of". When a whole sentence follows, it means "afraid that": "Jeg er bange for, at det er sandt" (I am afraid it is true).

banko.explanation: "Banko" means "bingo". When someone wins, they say the word out loud: "Hvem vandt?" "Det gjorde jeg. Banko!" (Who won? I did. Bingo!)

barberskum.explanation: "Barberskum" means "shaving foam". It is built from "at barbere" (to shave) and "skum" (foam). The same "skum" is in "et skumbad" (a bubble bath).

bare.explanation: "Bare" means "just". When you tell someone they may go ahead, it means "go ahead": "Kom bare ind" (Come on in). When you say an amount is small, it means "only": "Jeg har bare to timer" (I only have two hours).

bark.explanation: "En bark" means "bark", as in the outside of a tree. Do not mix it up with the sound a dog makes, "at gø" (to bark): "Hunden begynder at gø" (The dog starts to bark).

barmhjertighed.explanation: "Barmhjertighed" means "mercy". This word has no article, so leave out "en": "Dommeren viste barmhjertighed" (The judge showed mercy).

barsel.explanation: "Barsel" means "parental leave". Both mothers and fathers can take it: "Han er på barsel" (He is on parental leave).

barsk.explanation: "Barsk" means "harsh". When you describe a person's voice, use it too: "en barsk stemme" (a harsh voice). When you describe wild nature, use it: "en barsk natur" (a harsh landscape).

basilikum.explanation: "Basilikum" means "basil". This word has no article: "Vi har basilikum i haven" (We have basil in the garden).

basketball.explanation: "Basketball" means "basketball". When you mean the ball, add "en": "Jeg har købt en basketball" (I bought a basketball).

bedre.explanation: "Bedre" means "better". When you say you feel better after being ill, say: "Jeg har det bedre" (I feel better).

bedre sent end aldrig.explanation: "Bedre sent end aldrig" means "better late than never". When someone arrives late, you can answer them: "Undskyld, jeg er sen." "Bedre sent end aldrig." (Sorry, I am late. Better late than never.)

bedring.explanation: "En bedring" means "a recovery". When something other than health gets better, it means "an improvement": "en bedring i økonomien" (an improvement in the economy).

bedst.explanation: "Bedst" means "best". When you say what you like best, use "kan bedst lide" (like best): "Jeg kan bedst lide kaffe" (I like coffee best).

bedst før.explanation: "Bedst før" means "best before". Do not mix it up with "sidste anvendelsesdato" (use-by date): "Sidste anvendelsesdato er i dag" (The use-by date is today).

bedsteforældre.explanation: "Bedsteforældre" means "grandparents". It is built from "bedste" (best) and "forældre" (parents).

bedøvet.explanation: "Bedøvet" means "anesthetized". When someone is dazed after a shock, it means "stunned": "Hun var bedøvet af chok" (She was stunned by the shock).

begavet.explanation: "Begavet" means "gifted". For a person with a talent in one skill, use "talentfuld" (talented) instead: "en talentfuld pianist" (a talented pianist).

begge.explanation: "Begge" means "both of them". It is only for two: "Begge er her" (Both are here). When you mean any number of people, use "alle" (everyone): "Alle er her" (Everyone is here). When you add "to" (two), the meaning stays the same: "Jeg kender dem begge to" (I know both of them).

begrænset.explanation: "Begrænset" means "limited". When you say there is only a little room, use it before the noun: "begrænset plads" (limited space). It comes from "en grænse" (a border).

begær.explanation: "Et begær" means "a desire". When you name what is desired, add "efter" (for): "begær efter anerkendelse" (desire for recognition).

behagelig.explanation: "Behagelig" means "comfortable". When you describe a voice or a temperature, it means "pleasant": "en behagelig stemme" (a pleasant voice), "en behagelig temperatur" (a pleasant temperature).

behjælpelig.explanation: "Behjælpelig" means "helpful". It comes from "en hjælp" (a help). When you describe someone who helped you, say: "Han var meget behjælpelig" (He was very helpful).
